nutshell: Existing ReID research is fragmented into predefined scenario pairs (visible-infrared, aerial-ground, multi-modality), each needing its own task-specific model, which doesn't match real deployments where a query can come from any camera/modality against a gallery spanning everything. This paper defines Any-Scenario ReID (AS-ReID) - one model, any query, any heterogeneous gallery - introduces WHU-MARS (a 2,337-identity, 434,620-image tri-spectral aerial-ground dataset covering day/night/season/weather) to benchmark it, and proposes UAD, a single-branch framework that aligns per-identity features across modalities (ProCA) while enforcing global inter-identity margins via momentum-updated prototypes (GPD).
contributions: Formalizes Any-Scenario ReID (AS-ReID) as a unified task: a scenario is a (modality, viewpoint) pair, and a single shared model must retrieve correctly across a gallery spanning every scenario, with traditional/aerial-ground/visible-infrared/multi-modality ReID recovered as special-case restrictions of the same formulation.

WHU-MARS: a new multispectral aerial-ground benchmark (RGB/NIR/TIR from both ground cameras and UAV platforms, 2,337 identities, 434,620 images, spanning day/night, multiple seasons, and varied weather) with tri-spectral coverage per identity - by the paper's own comparison table, the largest multispectral person ReID dataset to date, released in two official splits (WHU-MARS-1000 and the full WHU-MARS-2337).

Unified Alignment and Discrimination (UAD): Progressive Center Alignment (ProCA) pools multi-view features into per-modality centers, then pulls those modality centers toward a shared identity anchor, reducing scenario-specific feature scatter without pairwise/quadratic-in-scenarios alignment losses. Global Prototype Discrimination (GPD) contrasts each sample against a momentum-updated, dataset-wide identity-prototype memory (not just in-batch negatives), enforcing large inter-identity margins under the abundant hard negatives that a heterogeneous gallery introduces.

Benchmarks UAD and a wide range of general/AG/VI-specific ReID methods across four protocols (AS-, AG-, VI-, MM-ReID) on WHU-MARS, with UAD achieving the best or most competitive results on most settings using the fewest parameters among the Transformer-based competitors.
deficiencies: The paper's own Table 7 benchmarks 9 published MM-ReID methods on WHU-MARS-1000 but never reports UAD's own performance under the MM-ReID protocol - despite MM-ReID being one of the four protocols the paper claims WHU-MARS supports 'within a single benchmark,' and despite UAD results being reported for the other three (AS-, AG-, VI-ReID). This is a real gap in an otherwise comprehensive four-protocol evaluation.

On the more standard VI-ReID metric (Table 5, NIR-to-RGB), UAD is not actually the best method - PMT beats it by a real margin (Rank-1 27.12 vs. 25.53, mAP 18.16 vs. 16.58), using two modality-specific models rather than UAD's single shared one. UAD only leads on the harder TIR-to-RGB protocol. The text's framing ('our unified UAD model remains competitive... in contrast, on the more difficult TIR-RGB protocol, UAD attains the best results') is accurate but doesn't explicitly name this as the single-model-convenience-vs-peak-accuracy tradeoff that it is.

Table 2 shows both official dataset versions actually train on the same number of identities (1,000) - WHU-MARS-2337's additional identities (1,337 more) only expand the *evaluation* gallery/query pool, not the training set. The paper's framing as 'the largest multispectral ReID dataset to date' could easily be read as implying proportionally more training data is available in the larger version, when the training-set scale is identical between both official splits.

All 434,620 images come from a single university campus (two UAV platforms, five ground nodes) over one continuous collection campaign (July-January). Despite genuine day/night/season/weather diversity within that campaign, there's no cross-site validation - it's untested whether a model trained on WHU-MARS generalizes to a physically different deployment (different camera hardware, UAV altitude range, or urban layout), which matters given the paper's explicit framing around 'real-world-aligned' and 'deployment-aligned' benchmarking.
notable: The dataset collection explicitly builds in privacy mitigations - on-site notices posted during capture, and automatic face mosaicking with no personally identifiable metadata retained - which is a genuinely good practice worth flagging given how many other papers in this corpus study either privacy-preserving ReID or explicitly surveillance/tracking-oriented ReID with no such discussion; this dataset paper handles it by design rather than as an afterthought. Also notable: Table 6's full 3x3 modality-pair breakdown of the single UAD model (not just the two pairs highlighted in the main VI-ReID comparison) is a more complete diagnostic than most multi-modal ReID papers in this batch bother to report, clearly showing TIR-involving pairs are uniformly the hardest (TIR-to-TIR intra-modality Rank-1 of only 20.98% is the best of any TIR-involving cell) - useful reference data for anyone building on this dataset.
